sections.heading: SUPERHERO GAMING
sections.text: Armed with these rules and handfuls of dice, you now have everything you need to play the game. The thing about roleplaying is that there’s much more to playing the game than what you can find in any book. Like chess, go, or poker, knowing the rules is only the first step when it comes to running a roleplaying game. sections.heading: CREATING VILLAINS
sections.text: Of all the characters GMs have to create, Villains are the most important. While roleplaying games have a long and venerable history of presenting Heroes with enemies to defeat, Villains are more than that. At their core, superhero stories—at least the ones that inspired this game—are about people doing the right thing. As characters who do the wrong thing, Villains provide the contrast that makes these stories work. Like Heroes, these characters represent who we can be, but they act as warnings rather than inspiration. As a result, even the lowliest Villains should be important characters in your game. As discussed in Chapter 2, Villains are created like Heroes. The rules are the same, but you don’t bother with Hero Points. You simply give these characters whatever Abilities, Talents, Powers, Perks, gear, and whatever else you want them to have. Some GMs like to know how many Hero Points their Villains would cost as Heroes, but that isn’t necessary (and often leads to maniacal laughter). That aside, the main difference between Heroes and Villains is their finishing touches. Although the following rules refer only to Villains, they also apply to Foes and Extras who turn out to be not so nice (Extras who fall on the side of the angels use the heroic motivations in Chapter 2).

sections.heading: VILLAIN MOTIVATIONS
sections.text: Like Heroes, Villains have motivations that make them do what they do. Some are quite different from those available to Heroes, while others are closer than you might think. In the end, a Villain’s motivation is not necessarily what makes them a Villain, but it is what drives them. As always, feel free to create your own villainous motivations if you can’t find what you need.

sections.heading: BOND
sections.text: The character has a powerful bond with someone who happens to be a Villain, so they’re along for the ride. This bond can be anything from strong kinship to warm affection to deep and abiding love. Or it might be the obsessive fixation of the truly unhinged because, you know, Villains. Some characters with this motivation are just as nasty as the person they care about, maybe even more so, while others are too broken, naïve, weak willed, or young to do anything but follow their lead. A few are not really Villains at all, but they will do anything necessary to protect the person they care about. straight flush in the process.

sections.heading: CONVICTION
sections.text: The Villain is pursuing what they deem to be the only reasonable course of action, or perhaps they feel obligated or duty-bound to do so. While they may not be especially evil or selfish, Villains with this motivation are often amoral and will do whatever is necessary to accomplish their goals. Archetypal characters with this motivation include the robot that gains sentience and concludes that humanity must be destroyed and the noble servant or soldier duty-bound to an ignoble superior.

sections.heading: DESPERATION
sections.text: The character is a Villain because they have a problem that can’t be solved any other way, or because they are being coerced into it by someone else. They might have developed powers they need to learn to control. Perhaps they were dying, and their powers are the byproduct of some magical or technological process that saved their life. Maybe they need super-powered help to save someone they love, or to protect themselves from someone or something. Someone may be using the threat of harming the character’s loved ones or revealing their terrible secret to force them into villainy. Or maybe they’re just trying to find someplace where they’ll be accepted rather than seen as a freak or a monster.

sections.heading: INSANITY/INSTINCT
sections.text: The Villain is insane and driven by delusions, or not fully in control of themselves and driven by destructive impulses, instincts, or programming. Animals, lunatics, monsters, robots, the undead, and other mindless engines of destruction often have this motivation. Villains with this motivation may or may not be sentient, and some aren’t Villains in any real sense except that the Heroes must stop them. For example, an enraged bear wounded and left to die by irresponsible hunters would have this motivation.

sections.heading: MALICE
sections.text: The character is motivated by sheer malice. The best of these Villains are mean and selfish, angry and entitled, or lacking in any real sense of empathy. The worst are truly evil or criminally insane: arsonists who want to watch the world burn, sociopaths who feel nothing for anyone but themselves, psychopaths who kill for the sheer joy of it, and lunatics who want people to see that life is just one big killing joke. Supernatural monsters like demons, devils, and vampires often have this motivation as well.

sections.heading: MONEY
sections.text: The Villain is in it for the money. For these career criminals, villainy is just a job that pays well. This motivation covers arms dealers, assassins, bank robbers, drug dealers, hired muscle, kidnappers, mercenaries, thieves of every kind, and entrepreneurs with shady business dealings. Villains with this motivation are typically practical, caring mainly about themselves and their bank accounts. More immoral than evil, Villains with this motivation sometimes have lines they won’t cross.

sections.heading: POWER
sections.text: The character wants to rule. Some have a lust for power, but others do so out of a sense of responsibility or manifest destiny. This is the motivation of conquerors, great military leaders with armies of henchmen willing to do their bidding. It also covers those who prefer to obtain power by more indirect means, such as by amassing extraordinary wealth, manipulating existing political systems (maybe even by running for office), or securing the power of popular opinion through mass media. These Villains will do anything to expand their reach while protecting the power they already possess.

sections.heading: PROGRESS
sections.text: The character will do anything in the name of progress or personal development. This is the motivation of mad geniuses willing to cast ethics aside in the name of science, single-minded explorers who will do anything to make a new discovery, and soul-corrupted sorcerers who will stop at nothing to uncover arcane secrets. While the desire for knowledge is a noble pursuit, characters with this motivation will go to any lengths to achieve this end, making them as dangerous as any zealot.

sections.heading: REBELLION
sections.text: The Villain refuses to play by society’s rules. These characters aren’t usually after money, power, or even thrills. They just don’t care, or maybe they’re trying to make a point. The Villains who truly don’t care tend to be aimless rebels who rarely have a larger plan in mind. They take what they want and do what they want because they can. The ones who want to send a message or incite change, on the other hand, can be as calculating and strategic as anyone else. Some of these Villains are hardcore punks who’ve spent their lives laughing at the sheep, while others were part of the flock until they snapped, pushed too far by a supervisor, spouse, or server at a fast food restaurant.

sections.heading: REVENGE
sections.text: The Villain is on a quest for revenge for some real or imagined wrong committed against them or someone they love. Some of these characters are monsters, but others are sympathetic, people pushed over the edge by grief, despair, or powerlessness. While some of these poor souls can be brought back from the abyss, others are too consumed with rage to ever turn back. For them, revenge is all there is.

sections.heading: THRILLS
sections.text: An adrenaline junkie primarily, the character is just having fun. Of course, their version of fun involves breaking the law and putting others in danger, but they don’t care about that. Villains with this motivation can seem harmless or even charming, and some in fact are, especially those who are young and immature. But the ones who should know better are often little more than self-centered sociopaths, focused on having fun regardless of how their actions hurt others.

sections.heading: ZEALOTRY
sections.text: The character is completely devoted to a cause or belief, whether noble or ignoble, and will cross any line in furtherance of their zealotry. Or they might espouse the twisted ideals of a particularly vile people, group, or nation. Villains with this motivation often act in concert with others who share their beliefs, sometimes even leading groups, nations, or worlds as their exemplar.

sections.heading: VILLAIN GOALS
sections.text: Instead of connections, Villains have goals, specific things they want to accomplish. While a Villain’s motivation tells you what drives them, their goals explain how they intend to satisfy those drives. Some Villains will have simple unimaginative goals: get rich by robbing a few banks, make enough money working as muscle for the mob to get their ailing spouse that experimental new treatment, etc. Others will have intricate, step-by-step goals spanning weeks, months, or even years, the kind needed to bring their master plan to fruition. And many will fall somewhere between these extremes. Smarter Villains usually have more complex and well-defined goals, but that isn’t always the case. At the end of the day, it all depends on the Villain, what they want to accomplish, and how they intend to get it done.

sections.heading: VILLAIN METHODS
sections.text: Instead of details, Villains have methods. This describes how the Villain operates and how far they’ll go to accomplish their goals. Does the Villain prefer to act directly, or do they work through others? If they act through others, are those characters allies, subordinates, or clueless catspaws? Does the Villain operate openly, do they move in secret, or are they hiding in plain sight? Do they tend to approach challenges physically, intellectually, or socially? What are the Villain’s usual tactics in combat? How do they prefer to fight, assuming they fight at all? A Villain’s methods also indicate what they are willing to do. Obviously, breaking the law isn’t an issue. But what about innocents: is the Villain willing to endanger, harm, or kill innocent civilians? Do they try to avoid this at all costs? Or do they fall somewhere in between? What about those foolish enough to stand in their way? Are they treated any differently than those smart enough to cower in fear or stand aside? And when someone does attempt to challenge the Villain, do they distinguish between mundane law enforcement personnel and super-powered interlopers?

sections.heading: VILLAINOUS ORIGINS
sections.text: The last element of every great Villain is their origin. As with Heroes, a Villain’s origin explains who they are and how they acquired their unique abilities. The best villainous origins, however, do one more thing: they make even the worst Villain somewhat sympathetic. A thoroughly despicable Villain is fine, but a thoroughly despicable Villain the players can relate to or have sympathy for is a masterpiece! It works that way in fiction, and it works that way in the game. The most interesting Villains are those we understand, no matter how much we abhor their actions. If you can make the players (that’s the players, not the Heroes) feel sympathy for the worst of your Villains, it will take your game to another level.

sections.heading: NEMESES
sections.text: There are Villains and there are nemeses. It’s easy to think of a nemesis as nothing more than a recurring Villain that really has it out for a particular Hero, but that would be a mistake. Although they are recurring Villains, a nemesis serves a unique purpose. While most Villains exist to challenge the Heroes, nemeses exist to help define them. A nemesis is always a dark reflection of their heroic archrival. For some, this means the two share something essential in common. They might have identical abilities and powers, backgrounds, goals, methods, motivations, origin stories, or weaknesses. These kinds of nemeses highlight the fact that people have choices. Regardless of their similarities, one of these characters became a Hero and one became a Villain. Their choices were not the inevitable result of anything they have in common; they came from within and speak volumes about who these people are. The other kind of nemesis is one that embodies the exact opposite of something essential to their heroic archenemy. Here, the conflict between Hero and Villain reflects a larger conflict between two broader concepts, ideals, or philosophies: strength versus intellect, freedom versus order, light versus darkness, capitalism versus communism, and so on. In some cases, neither concept is inherently right or wrong; how they’re pursued is what separates Hero from Villain. In others, the difference between good and evil couldn’t be more obvious. Because Heroes and their nemeses are so closely intertwined, players (not GMs) create nemeses for their Heroes. Players who aren’t interested in creating a nemesis can leave this to the GM, or they can choose not to have one. The decision is entirely up to each player. Once a player creates their nemesis, that character belongs to the GM and is treated like any other Villain. GMs should follow the guidelines and suggestions a player establishes when creating their nemesis, but once created, control of the nemesis rests squarely in the hands of the GM.

sections.heading: FOES
sections.text: Everything discussed above applies as much to Foes as it does to Villains. Mechanically, the only difference between Foes and Villains is that Foes have less Health (usually half as much). Although Foes tend to be less developed than Villains, the difference between the two often boils down to which character has the spotlight at the moment. Many comic book supervillains have been both Villain and Foe over the years, hopping back and forth between roles depending on how central they are to the story. While this kind of flexibility isn’t usually an element of roleplaying games, it’s very common in comic books and easy enough to replicate in P&P by making these characters Villains in some stories and Foes in others. While perhaps not every supervillain should get this treatment, it will go a long way to ensuring that Foes are just as interesting as Villains.

sections.heading: SUPER TIP!
sections.text: Superhero games become stale villain-ofthe-week slugfests if the Heroes don’t have personal lives that let them be real people as well as caped crusaders. No matter how noble, steadfast, or invulnerable the Heroes, they should always have flawed, fickle, fragile people in their lives who they care about dearly.

sections.heading: PLOT
sections.text: Once you have a Villain or Villains, decide on a plot. At this point in the process, the plot is just a simple phrase or sentence that describes what the story is going to be about. Most superhero plots fall into one of three categories: schemes, plans, or events. Each is described below.

sections.heading: SCHEMES
sections.text: A scheme is a nefarious plot the Villain or Villains intend to carry out. Most of the time, the Heroes must stop a scheme from coming to fruition. Occasionally, the scheme has already been accomplished when the story begins, in which case the Heroes have to deal with the aftermath, figure out how to repair or undo whatever the Villains have done, or both. This is probably the most common plot for a superhero story because Heroes tend to be reactive, responding only when reasonably certain that the Villains have done, are doing, or intend to do something illegal.

sections.heading: PLOTS — PLANS
sections.text: The opposite of a scheme, a plan is something the Heroes set out to do, either of their own accord or at the behest of some other person or organization. In this case, the Villains are the ones attempting to foil the plan and prevent the Heroes from accomplishing their goal. Sometimes, the reasons for this are obvious; other times, figuring out why the Villains are involved is part of the story.

sections.heading: PLOTS — EVENTS
sections.text: Events are major occurrences that the Heroes become involved in, but which can’t be attributed to the Heroes or the Villains, at least not directly or not intentionally. Although Villains often become involved in these plots, they’re usually reacting to or taking advantage of whatever is happening. If the event is especially catastrophic, the Villains might even put aside their differences and try to help the Heroes. After all, you can’t conquer the Earth if there’s no Earth left to conquer.

sections.heading: TROPES
sections.text: The next thing to consider when creating a story is which tropes you want to use. Tropes are narrative elements common to a genre, in this case the superhero genre. Although not necessary, tropes can help make your game feel more like a comic book. Besides, there are so many great superhero tropes to choose from that it seems a shame not to take advantage of them. You can pick from the list below or use any of the countless others we’re sure to have missed.

sections.heading: AMNESIA
sections.text: One or more of the Heroes lose their memory for at least some portion of the story. They won’t know who they are or whom they can trust. They might not even remember they have superpowers. Or they might think they’re supervillains, typically because some Villain tricks them into believing this, at least until the Heroes uncover the truth thanks to their unflinching moral compasses.

sections.heading: APES AND/OR DINOSAURS
sections.text: The story involves apes, dinosaurs, or both. If it involves apes, they’re intelligent apes, as least as intelligent and/or technologically advanced as human beings if not more so. If it involves dinosaurs, the dinosaurs may or may not be intelligent time travelers—this one can go either way.

sections.heading: ATLANTIS
sections.text: Whether bearing that name or another, just about every comic book universe includes an undersea kingdom hidden away from humanity for most of history. The story is going to involve this kingdom and its people in some way, whether as allies, enemies, or both.

sections.heading: BACK FROM THE DEAD
sections.text: The Villain of the story turns out to be an old archrival the Heroes thought was dead. Or perhaps it’s an imposter. If it does turn out to be an imposter, the true Villain (again, supposedly dead) may make a brief cameo, drawn out of hiding to crush any who would dare take their name. This trope works best with a Villain the Heroes have faced in the past, ideally on multiple occasions.

sections.heading: BETRAYED
sections.text: Curse your inevitable betrayal! The Heroes are betrayed in some way by a former ally. The treacherous former ally may or may not become one of the enemies the Heroes have to defeat later in the story. The Heroes may eventually discover that the former ally was acting under duress, but it’s just as likely that the former ally really was a bad guy all along. Although this trope often is used together with the Unlikely Ally trope (see below), it’s almost too obvious to be worth it. Almost.

sections.heading: CAPTURED
sections.text: The Heroes get captured and must somehow escape their confinement. Of course, for one reason or another, their Powers won’t be of any use. For a real change of pace, the story might start with the Heroes already in captivity—they might not even remember how they got there. Give each Hero 1 Resolve as a peace offering for using this heavy-handed trope.

sections.heading: DEATHTRAPS
sections.text: Deathtraps are the Captured trope on performance enhancers. The Heroes not only get captured; they also get placed in a deathtrap from which they have to escape. This admittedly corny trope has fallen out of favor. Honestly, if a Villain wants to kill a Hero they have at their mercy, there are easier ways than tossing them into a tank that gradually fills with water, lowering them into a vat of acid, tying them under a massive weight that will slowly crush them, etc. Plus, deathtraps tend to be most effective on Heroes who lack true superpowers (although you can get around this with power nullifiers). But if the trope fits the game, the deathtrap is a classic worth dusting off.

sections.heading: EVIL DUPLICATES
sections.text: The Heroes must confront their (presumably evil) duplicates in the story. These duplicates might be clones or robots meant to publicly misbehave and discredit the Heroes. They might be doppelgangers from an alternate dimension, or perhaps from a Future Gone Wrong that the Heroes need to fix. They might be mental constructs created by some cosmic entity. Or they might be something else. The specifics matter less than the fact that the Heroes will have to battle themselves.

sections.heading: GRUDGE MATCH
sections.text: One or more of the Villains in this story are characters the Heroes have gone up against in the past. They might have broken their way out of prison, they might have been hired by someone because of their prior history with the Heroes, they might be doing something specifically to get back at the Heroes, or their presence might be nothing more than a bad coincidence. Whatever the case, the Villains have a bone to pick with the Heroes and are itching for a rematch.

sections.heading: HERO VS HERO
sections.text: The Heroes must fight other superheroes at some point during the story. This could happen for any number of reasons, often mind control, mistaken identity, or misunderstanding. To be honest, the real reason for this is that comic book fans seem to love having superheroes fight each other. Assuming the other superheroes haven’t turned to the dark side, things should be cleared up and everyone should be more or less friends again by the time the story concludes.

sections.heading: HOSTAGE CRISIS
sections.text: The Villain takes someone hostage, ideally someone important to one or more of the Heroes. The Heroes have to rescue this person by the time the story concludes and may need to be very careful about how they do this because the Villain will use the hostage as leverage. Occasionally, the Heroes will discover that what they thought was a hostage was in fact an accomplice (see Betrayed and Willing Victim).

sections.heading: INNOCENT BYSTANDERS
sections.text: At least one major scene is going to take place in a location choked with so many civilians the Villains won’t know what to do with themselves. If it’s a battle scene, the Heroes are going to have their hands full protecting these people. If it’s an investigation or a roleplaying scene, the threat of what might happen to all those innocent people will force the Heroes to stand down while the Villains cross something off their evil to-do list, escape with a hostage, gloat insufferably, or do something equally infuriating.

sections.heading: THE LOST WORLD
sections.text: The story takes place in some lost primeval world. It often involves protecting a tribe of peaceful—and usually attractive— natives from a different tribe of warlike—and usually less attractive—natives or protecting the lost world itself from exploitation. Occasionally, the twist is that the attractive and initially friendly natives are actually complete jerks who are using and abusing their less evolved neighbors. And sometimes, the Heroes must protect the lost world and its inhabitants from being exploited by the people who sent them there in the first place.

sections.heading: MANIPULATED
sections.text: The Heroes discover that they’ve been lied to or are being manipulated by someone they trusted, often an employer, authority figure, or Patron. This trope can be particularly effective if the Heroes all have the same Patron, and this person or organization turns out to have been lying to them or telling them half-truths. It becomes even more interesting when different Heroes have different degrees of loyalty to the Patron. This trope is just a specific version of Betrayed.

sections.heading: THE MISUNDERSTOOD VILLAIN
sections.text: The Villain turns out to be misunderstood rather than evil. This is often the case when the Villain is a wild animal or rampaging monster of some kind. Other common scenarios include Villains who are being blackmailed, completely unaware of the harm they’re causing, or under someone else’s control.

sections.heading: PLOT TWIST
sections.text: The Heroes learn something, or some new development occurs that either changes the goal they were originally trying to accomplish or brings a new goal into play. This new or additional goal is normally more difficult, more dangerous, or of greater consequence than the original.

sections.heading: POWERLESS
sections.text: The Heroes are rendered powerless for all or a portion of the story and must accomplish their goals without relying on their unique abilities. Or they could be surrounded by other people— maybe including people they know—and must pretend to be civilians for most of the story. This can make for an interesting game and a great change of pace, but don’t do this too early in a series. Let the players enjoy their superpowers for a while before you strip them away.

sections.heading: RELATIONSHIP
sections.text: One or more of the Heroes has a significant personal relationship with someone involved in the story, often a victim or a Villain (or better yet, one of each). Even if the Villain has a secret identity, the Hero or Heroes will know or strongly suspect their true identity.

sections.heading: REVERSE WORLD
sections.text: The story takes place on a planet or dimension that is the mirror image of the “real” one. In that world, the Heroes are the bad guys and the Villains are the superheroes. The Heroes may need to team up with characters who are normally their enemies to fight those who are normally their allies. They might even have to fight themselves (see Evil Duplicates). This is another technique that won’t work if you do it too early in a series. The players need to get to know their Heroes, the Villains, and the important Extras in their world before you turn everything upside down.

sections.heading: SECRET BASE
sections.text: Some part of the story involves finding, reaching, exploring, escaping from, or destroying a Villain’s secret base. The base is likely to be found in a hazardous, remote, or unusual location like in the Arctic or the Antarctic, on an uncharted island, deep under the ocean, in a volcano, on a satellite orbiting the Earth or another planet in the Solar System, on the Moon, or in a parallel or pocket dimension, etc. For a change of pace, rather than being in active use, the base has long-since been abandoned.

sections.heading: SECRET MISSION
sections.text: Something about what the Heroes are doing must remain secret from one of the NPCs, the authorities, or the public. The Heroes might have to guard someone who can’t know they’re being guarded. They might be tasked with something too big or too dangerous for ordinary police. They could be saddled with a job so critical that the general public must be kept in the dark because there would be widespread panic and rioting in the streets in they knew the danger they were in. You get the idea. Whatever the case, keeping the secret is going to be easier said than done.

sections.heading: STAKES RAISED
sections.text: Save the cheerleader, save the world. The Heroes learn something, or some new development occurs that significantly raises the stakes of the current story, making it that much more critical that the Heroes succeed. A common version of this trope is that what initially seems to be an ordinary crime turns out to be the first step in a Villain’s larger master plan.

sections.heading: STUPID HUMOR
sections.text: Something about what the Heroes must do is absurd or ridiculous. If the Heroes must participate in a contest, it’s going to involve something like ballroom roller skating or fullcontact macramé. If they must rescue a hostage, it’s going to be a magically animated Teddy Bear with a colorful vocabulary. Although these stories tend to be more lighthearted than most, this trope works best if everything else in the story remains just as serious as in any other game. The contrast is what makes this work.

sections.heading: THIRD PARTY
sections.text: A third party that favors neither the Heroes nor the Villains enters the story. This third party has its own agenda that may put it in conflict with the Heroes, the Villains, or both. The Heroes and Villains may even need to put their differences aside and work together against this third party.

sections.heading: TIME LIMIT
sections.text: Although Heroes rarely take it easy, they’re really going to be racing against the clock in this story. Often, the Villain has set wheels in motion and their master plan will reach a point of no return if the Heroes can’t stop it by a certain time. Occasionally, the Heroes are competing against the Villains—or maybe against a group of rival superheroes—and need to do something or get somewhere first.

sections.heading: TIME TRAVEL
sections.text: The Heroes have to travel to the past, the future, or both over the course of this story, or they’re going to meet characters from those times, often characters related to them in some way. This trope can involve a host of time travel hijinks, from the comedic like going to the past to make sure your parents meet, to the sobering like going to the future to discover global apocalypse and ruin.

sections.heading: TRUE VILLAIN
sections.text: The Heroes learn something or some new development occurs that makes it evident that the original Villain is actually a cat’s paw or a patsy for the true Villain, who is usually more dangerous than the original. The Heroes often have to defeat the original Villain before this is revealed.

sections.heading: UNDERCOVER WORK
sections.text: The Heroes have to go undercover, often but not always among Villains. Should that be the case, the Heroes may get to see a different side of Villains they usually can’t stand, and might even grow to empathize if not actually like some of them. As with several of the tropes described in this section, this one works best after the players and their Heroes have gotten to know—and ideally really grown to despise—a particular Villain or group of Villains.

sections.heading: UNLIKELY ALLY
sections.text: The Heroes encounter an unexpected or unlikely ally, possibly even a Villain, who will help them in some way, at least in this story. In fact, it’s possible that this unlikely ally is the one who comes to the Heroes for help in the first place. This unlikely alliance may be a one-time thing, or it could signal the beginning of a different relationship between the ally and the Heroes (a Villain who becomes a Hero, for example, which happens all the time in comic books).

sections.heading: UNSTOPPABLE FOE
sections.text: The Heroes face an enemy they can’t defeat. This could take the form of a being from beyond who whisks them away to do battle for its amusement, an ancient cosmic entity that must consume planets to survive, a massive invasion force they can’t hope to withstand, or something similar. The Heroes will have to use diplomacy, cunning, or guile against this opponent, or they may simply need to flee for now until they can find a way to overcome this enemy in a future story.

sections.heading: WILLING VICTIM
sections.text: Someone the Heroes are attempting to rescue or save is in league with the Villains and will betray or attempt to thwart the Heroes to the best of their ability. This technique works best if the victim is someone important to one or more of the Heroes, especially if the supposed victim turns out to be the major Villain of the story. This is just a specific version of the Betrayed trope.

sections.heading: WORLD GONE MAD
sections.text: The world is not as it should be. Perhaps it’s been transformed into a land resembling something out of medieval fantasy, perhaps it’s become a post-apocalyptic wasteland, perhaps the machines have taken over, or perhaps it’s as one would expect if things had worked out differently at some critical juncture in history. The Heroes may or may not realize that things are not as they should be, although the players sure will. This trope can serve as the backdrop for a single story or for a story arc that spans multiple adventures and culminates with the Heroes doing whatever they must to return things to normal.

sections.heading: SACRIFICE
sections.text: Personal sacrifice is probably the most ignored or forgotten element of the superhero genre, at least when it comes to roleplaying games. This is unfortunate because it’s more important than just about anything else. Sacrifice is what makes a superhero game feel like a superhero game instead of a game about people who just happen to have powers. It’s the greatest source of conflict and drama in comic books, because sacrificing yourself for others is what it means to be a hero (super or not). Typically, the kind of personal sacrifice we’re talking about occurs when a story presents a Hero with a choice between doing the right thing and doing the easy thing. Inevitably, the right thing is the heroic thing—dangerous, selfless, and probably thankless. The easy thing, on the other hand, is what the Hero would rather do. It’s comfortable, safe, and often in the character’s best interest. But it’s not what a hero would do. Heroes who do the right thing often suffer personally or professionally and must live with the fallout of ignoring their relationships, careers, etc. Occasionally, the sacrifice involves only the character’s life as a superhero, like having to choose between saving a friend or saving a building full of strangers, or having to resist killing a Villain who did something terrible to the Hero or someone they love. For example, what do you do when a supervillain attacks the city on your wedding anniversary? What if it’s not a supervillain, just an ordinary bunch of bank robbers? Can’t the cops handle that? What if you and your spouse are going through a tough time? Don’t you deserve a chance to fix things? With everything you do for the city, don’t you deserve a chance to be happy too? This type of drama gives characters a chance to truly be heroic, not because they have incredible abilities, but because they do the right thing, even when it requires great personal sacrifice. By adding these moments of sacrifice to the game, GMs give players the opportunity to roleplay what it means to be a true hero, to put some larger goal or greater good ahead of themselves. Or it lets them roleplay what it means to betray their principles, to give in to fear or pressure, to put themselves ahead of others, because sometimes even superheroes falter. Either way, these moments underscore the fact that this isn’t a game about adventurers with powers, this is a game about superheroes.

sections.heading: USING SACRIFICE
sections.text: Not every Hero should have to deal with personal sacrifice in every story. While comic books may be spandex-clad soap operas, they’re fiction and this is a game. GMs would need to have too much control over the story to keep creating opportunities for this kind of drama in their games. Instead, moments of personal sacrifice should usually be reserved for stories that spotlight an individual Hero and should involve only that Hero. In fact, the GM and the player can work together to come up with the conflict that triggers this drama, typically something involving the Hero’s motivation, connections, or details. Sacrifice should unfold over the course of a story in roughly four parts. In the first, the GM should introduce the conflict in a brief scene that involves only the Hero, or as part of a larger scene involving several Heroes. In the second part, something should happen to ramp up the tension, making it clear that there is no easy way for the Hero to resolve the situation. The Hero may seriously consider doing the wrong thing at this point in the story, but something will prevent this from happening. In the third part, which happens at some critical moment in the story, the Hero must make a hard choice. And in the fourth and final part, the Hero must deal with the consequences of their decision. For example, one way to handle the anniversary dinner example above would be as follows. In one scene, the Hero and their spouse have an argument or tense exchange indicating that there’s trouble (even better if this is an ongoing issue from a previous game). In a second scene, there might be an even bigger argument. Or you might have an interlude with another character (maybe while shopping for groceries) where the Hero talks about how they hope to mend fences at the anniversary dinner. The third scene happens on the way to dinner if not right in the middle of it, right when things are starting to look hopeful, duty calls, and the Hero has to make their choice. And the final scene involves the consequences of whatever choice the Hero made—a cold shoulder at home, or a news report about civilians being injured or even killed during the bank robbery the Hero decided to ignore.

sections.heading: MOOD AND SACRIFICE
sections.text: In games with darker moods, there’s no magic solution. Heroes who do the right thing and decide to take on the Villains, rescue the hostages, or save the world will suffer due to their choices. They might get seriously injured, their friends might cut them off, they might get fired, their spouse might leave them, their enemies might bribe or extort their way out of prison, and so on. In short, their good deeds won’t go unpunished. Heroes who choose not to make the necessary sacrifice will avoid these repercussions, but the guilt will be difficult to bear as they learn the terrible things that happened because they didn’t do anything about it. If they didn’t feel guilty, they wouldn’t be superheroes. In games with lighter moods, it’s assumed the Heroes will probably make the right decision, albeit after some soul searching. Of course, players are free to make whatever decision they wish. More importantly, the consequences of these decisions are typically temporary and less severe in games with lighter moods. Heroes who do the right thing might wind up wearing a cast for a scene or two, hurting the feelings of someone close to them, getting into hot water at work, and so on, but the consequences they face won’t be too bad or last too long. Similarly, Heroes who choose to act unheroically will probably fall into a short-lived funk, often until fate presents them with an opportunity to redeem themselves (this will almost certainly happen sooner rather than later in such games).

sections.heading: RESOLVE AND SACRIFICE
sections.text: You don’t need rules to bring the idea of personal sacrifice into your games. However, if you want to reinforce the impact of this drama on a Hero, use the following optional rules. If a Hero does the right thing, they immediately earn 1 to 3 Resolve (roll one die and halve the result). However, at some point during the next story, the GM brings the consequences of that decision into the game, and the Hero will immediately lose 2 to 4 Resolve (roll as above but add 1 to the result) as they deal with the fallout of their decision. If a Hero does the easy thing, they immediately earn 3 Resolve. However, from that moment on, all uses of Resolve costs twice as much as usual—guilt is not an easy thing to deal with—especially for a superhero. This lasts until the Hero finds redemption by doing something truly heroic.

sections.heading: SCENES
sections.text: At this point you have your Villain or Villains, a plot, and a few tropes, and you’ve decided whether to throw some moment of personal sacrifice into the story. It’s now time to create your scenes. Before we get to that, we should probably say a word two about scenes themselves. There are three basic kinds of scenes: action scenes, investigation scenes, and social scenes. Action scenes involve fights, chases, and other kinds of, well, action. Investigation scenes involve gathering information in various ways such as by exploring the world, interacting with NPCs, researching online or (heaven forbid) in actual books, and scouring locations for clues. Scenes in which players have to solve riddles or puzzles are usually investigation scenes. Social scenes focus on interpersonal interaction between characters. Interludes (discussed later in this chapter) are usually social scenes. Although often played purely for roleplaying purposes or to provide background information, social scenes can also involve challenges to overcome or information to uncover. It’s just that these things are accomplished by interacting with other characters in social scenes. Most stories should include a mix of all three types of scenes, although how much of each depends on your group. Some folks prefer lots of action, others enjoy solving mysteries and puzzles, and others want an abundance of freeform roleplaying. As with everything else, salt to taste. As you create each scene, include only as much detail as you need to feel comfortable. This varies by GM, by story, and by scene. An experienced GM might be comfortable running a complex story with only sketchy details, while a novice may want to do a lot of prep work for each scene. Both approaches are perfectly fine, as is anything between these extremes. However, there are a few guidelines that apply to just about everyone. You should always have the mechanical stuff worked out ahead of time, things like character stats and rough maps of areas where combat may occur. You should also know who your NPCs are, what they’re like, and what they want (their motivations). Beyond that, do only as much prep work as you need to run a great game.

sections.heading: THE CLIMAX
sections.text: The climax is the big finale, where the Heroes and the Villains go at one another in a no-holds-barred winner-takes-all showdown. Although it might seem strange, this is probably the first scene you should create. You need to know exactly where the Villains are headed, what their plans are, and what the culmination of their nefarious plot will look like. This is going to be the scene where you bring out the big guns and throw everything you have at the Heroes. The climax is usually an action scene, specifically a fight scene, but this doesn’t always have to be the case. Some Villains may have to be outsmarted rather than outfought, while others may need to be convinced of the error of their ways. And some climaxes will involve two or more of these elements. Whatever the specifics, the challenges the Heroes face in this scene should be the toughest the story has to offer. By the time this scene is done, the players—not the Heroes, the players— should be sweating. Despite everything above, don’t force the climax. If your players come up with a way to thwart the Villain before you reach the climax of the story, let them. Don’t steal their victory, assuming they’ll prefer the climax you had in mind. Trust us, they won’t. They’ll just feel cheated and disempowered when they realize their idea should have worked. Instead of railroading your players toward the grand finale you envisioned, save your ideas for a future story, and give them the victory they deserve.

sections.heading: THE HOOK
sections.text: The hook is the first scene of the story, and it’s usually the second scene you create. Once you know where the story’s going, the next thing to decide is how the Heroes get dragged into it. A good hook does three things: gets the players interested, tells them what they need to know, and draws the Heroes into the action—hooks are usually action scenes. These are listed in order of importance. Player interest is paramount. If the players aren’t excited about the story right from the start, you’re in for a long night. While the first scene of the story should also tell the players what they need to know and pull their Heroes into the action, these things are less critical. If your players are interested, they’ll find a way to get their Heroes involved in the story, and they’ll forgive you for any information you forgot to share. Get them hooked (see what we did there?) and everything else will follow. Most hooks occur at the beginning of the story. The Heroes are doing their own thing when someone or something comes along and pulls them into the action. This gives the players all the information they need right at the start. When starting a story at the beginning, throw the Heroes into the action as soon as possible. Never start a game with a painfully long monologue. Any introduction that demands more than five minutes of narrative on your part is probably a bust; the players will lose interest before the game even begins. Get the story moving and the players playing as soon as possible. If you want to try something different, start a story smack in the middle of a fight or a chase scene, something serious and dangerous. Give your players just enough information to understand what they need to accomplish, but not why. Then, once the scene is over, take a moment to explain what the Heroes were doing and why they were doing it. While this kind of hook does involve some railroading, it’s a great way to get the Heroes into the action and the players interested right away; few things make players sit up and take notice like putting their Heroes in danger. When starting a story like this, you have to take extra care to ensure that whatever you say happened before the hook makes logical sense within the game and is true to the Heroes. If your description of what happened before the story begins has the Heroes doing something stupid or out of character, your players won’t buy into your idea.

sections.heading: THE BODY
sections.text: Once you have your hook and your climax, you then create the other scenes that make up the body of your story. Don’t try to create a whole story all at once. Instead, just consider where the story might go after the hook, see where your imagination leads you, and create that scene (or scenes if the story can go in multiple directions). Then move on from there, thinking only about the scenes that might follow the ones you already created, remembering that they eventually need to lead to the story’s intended climax. While by no means mandatory, the typical superhero story structure often goes like this: Hook: often an action scene that pulls the Heroes into the story. Exposition: the call to adventure, this is an investigation or social scene in which the Heroes learn something about the story and set out to accomplish their goals. Action: an action scene more intense than the first that progresses the story. Rising Exposition: the stakes get raises, this is an investigation or social scene that not only moves the story forward but also ramps up the pace, stakes, or tension. Rising Action: an even more intense action scene, often one in which the Heroes suffer some kind of defeat or setback or learn something that makes their situation even more dire. Preparation: an investigation or social scene in which the Heroes learn what they need to accomplish their goals and everyone prepares for the final confrontation. If a Hero is being spotlighted in the story, this is often when that character must face a hard choice or personal sacrifice. Climax: usually the most intense action scene of the entire story, this is when the Heroes must confront the Villains and save the city or otherwise accomplish their goals. Finale: this brief social scene concludes the story and highlights any loose ends. Another way to think about your stories is in terms of pinch points and playgrounds. Pinch points are the scenes that must happen in the story, while playgrounds are the scenes that happen between pinch points. The hook, for example, is a pinch point that gets the story rolling. After that, the players are in the playground, and can take the story in any number of directions, depending on what they do. However, whatever they do, they will eventually find their way to the next pinch point, which then opens another playground of possibilities. And so forth, until you reach the climax. In most superhero games, pinch points tend to be action scenes. In stories of a more investigative bent, pinch points tend to be the scenes in which the Heroes stumble across the next Big Clue to whatever mystery they’re trying to solve. However you structure your story, most games should increase in pace and tension as the Heroes move through them. While no superhero story should start off slow, all stories should gain steam over time and be cooking with gas by the time you reach the climax. Similarly, the challenges faced by the Heroes (physical, mental, and social) should become more daunting as the story progresses. Scenes should also be of varying lengths and types. Some will be action oriented, often involving combat and a lot of dice rolling. Others will be intellectually oriented, with players making plans, solving puzzles, or unraveling mysteries. And others will be socially oriented, filled with character interaction

sections.heading: TRAPPINGS
sections.text: You’re just about done. The last thing you need to do is add a few trappings, little details that help bring the game world to life for your players. The two most important trappings are the Extras with whom the Heroes interact and the sets where your important scenes take place.

sections.heading: EXTRAS
sections.text: Although Villains and Foes are important characters in most stories, the Heroes are probably going to interact more with your Extras than with any other characters. That being the case, you should give your Extras as much detail as you need to bring them to life while playing the game. Important Extras should have the same finishing touches as Heroes or Villains (which one you use depends on the Extra) even if you don’t bother creating them as complete characters. You need to know who your Extras are to play them, but you don’t necessarily need to know everything they can do. As GM, you are literally playing everyone else on the planet (in the galaxy, the universe, etc.) so you might not be ready with a fully fleshed-out description when the players decide to strike up a conversation with some random NPC. If you find yourself in a pinch when describing an Extra, give them one or more distinctions to help create an interesting or memorable character on the fly.

sections.heading: SETS
sections.text: Sets are locations the Heroes will visit in the story. Although sets are often mapped out, that isn’t necessary. Some sets, such as those where a fight or an action scene is likely to occur, probably require at least some amount of detail, in which case preparing a map ahead of time is a good idea, but most require nothing more than a few choice descriptors. As with everything else, do only as much prep work as you need to feel comfortable. Whenever possible, choose dramatic, exotic, or unusual locations for your sets. Watch action movies and notice where their action scenes take place. Keep your eyes open for interesting places you can use as the basis for your sets. If you’re having trouble coming up with interesting sets, the following tables include generic locations and specific real-world locales. The best sets become part of the action, enhance the mood, and help make the game more compelling. When selecting your sets, think about how they can enhance the scenes in which they appear. For action scenes, try finding ways to bring your sets into the action. For investigation scenes, contemplate how you can make your sets part of the mystery, riddle, or puzzle. For social scenes, think about how your sets can ramp up the tension or the drama. Consider the following suggestions for making static sets come to life. Civilians: Crowds and traffic can make it difficult to get anywhere in a hurry and almost impossible to have a super-powered brawl without putting people in serious jeopardy. Dangers: Sets can include hazards such as barbed wire, downed power lines, explosive gas, hidden landmines, pools of lava, sheer drops, weak floors, traps, and tripwires. Derelict: A long-abandoned set that has fallen into a state of disrepair is both creepy and potentially dangerous. It can also do wonders to create a moody environment. Elevations: Always remember things like balconies, catwalks, ladders, overpasses, pits, ramps, and stairways. A set with varied elevations can make a rather boring fight much more interesting. Moving Parts: Factories, assembly lines, and other industrial sets should contain moving parts, busily—and often dangerously—going about their business while the Heroes do their thing. Noise: Background noise can add realism, underscore the mood, and act as another variable. A loud set can hamper communication and perception; a quiet one can create an eerie or unsettling mood. Obstacles: The Heroes may need to cross treacherous bridges, scale or tunnel under thick walls, swing across chasms, swim through water-filled passages, or squeeze through narrow spaces. Visibility: Lighting, darkness, fog, smoke, strobe lights, and anything else that impacts visibility can affect both the atmosphere and the tactical aspects of a set. Weather: Weather can affect both mood and game mechanics. Wind, rain, snow, ice, and fog all convey a certain mood, and can make things more difficult for the Heroes in one way or another.
