sections.heading: CREATING SERIES
sections.text: As mentioned earlier, a series is a group of related stories that get played out in order. In other games, this would be called a campaign. There’s no right way or wrong way to create a series. As with the previous section, this isn’t intended to teach you the one and only way to go about doing that. Instead, think of this section as a checklist of things to consider when creating a new series.

sections.heading: SETTING
sections.text: The setting refers to the world (physical and thematic) in which the game takes place. Some settings require more homework than others. A game set in our modern-day world doesn’t require a lot of prep. The same goes for a game set in any world you’re already familiar with, such as any of the major comic book universes. However, if you’re going to run a game set in an unfamiliar world, you’ll need to spend a little time creating it. Because this is an action-oriented roleplaying game, we suggest not going overboard. Create enough of the world to let your players get their bearings and make up the rest as you go, often by taking input from the players themselves. Whatever you decide, it’s important that you pick a setting everyone finds interesting. If you’re the only one of your friends who grooves on a particular setting, don’t set your game there. Some common superheroic settings are listed below.

sections.heading: ALTERNATE HISTORY
sections.text: The series takes place in a world like ours might have been had history been different, probably the most common example being if the Axis powers had won World War II.

sections.heading: CONTEMPORARY
sections.text: The easiest and most common setting for traditional comic book superheroes, the series takes place in our modern-day world, or in one very similar to the one we know.

sections.heading: CYBERPUNK
sections.text: The series is set in a dystopian near-future ruled by corporations and the wealthy elite and characterized by the ubiquity of cybernetics and the dehumanization they bring.

sections.heading: CYBERPUNK FANTASY
sections.text: Take a cyberpunk setting and add fantasy races, magic, and monsters to taste.

sections.heading: DIESELPUNK
sections.text: The series takes place in an often dystopian pulp era set between the World Wars and characterized by retro-futuristic diesel-powered technology and a pervasive art deco style.

sections.heading: EASTERN FANTASY
sections.text: The series is set in a fantasy world based on Arabian, Chinese, Indian, Japanese, Persian, or other Eastern cultures and mythologies, or an amalgam of them.

sections.heading: HIGH FANTASY
sections.text: The series is set in a medieval fantasy world based on Western mythology.

sections.heading: HISTORIC
sections.text: The series is set in our world at some point in history. Popular historic settings for comic book superheroes include the Old West, the Age of Sail, the Victorian Era, and World War II.

sections.heading: POST-APOCALYPTIC
sections.text: The series is set on our world or another after a devastating catastrophe, sometimes natural, but more often than not manmade (oh, the humanity).

sections.heading: PULP
sections.text: The series takes place in that two-fisted time between the 1920s and the 1930s. It’s kind of like Dieselpunk, but lighter in tone and without all the retro-fetishism.

sections.heading: RETRO-FUTURE
sections.text: The series is set in the somewhat whimsical future envisioned in much early science fiction. Think fishbowl helmets and ray guns with fins.

sections.heading: SCI-FI
sections.text: The series, which often takes place in our distant future, it set in a science fiction setting where things like aliens, faster-than-light travel, and laser weapons are commonplace.

sections.heading: STEAMPUNK
sections.text: The series is set in a fantastical Victorian Era (often one much less dystopian than the actual historical period) characterized by fantasy races, magic, and fantastical steam-powered technology.

sections.heading: SWORD-AND-PLANET
sections.text: The series is set on a primitive and barbaric world, often Mars or Venus, and characterized by quaint retro sci-fi technology envisioned by early twentieth-century authors.

sections.heading: SWORD-AND-SORCERY
sections.text: The series is set in a typically grim and barbaric fantasy world.

sections.heading: URBAN FANTASY
sections.text: The series takes place in our modern world, or one very much like it, but one in which magic, mythical creatures, and monsters are real.

sections.heading: WORLD-HOPPING
sections.text: The series has no single setting because, for whatever reason, the Heroes will travel to different worlds and/or times over the course of the series (oh boy).

sections.heading: PREMISE
sections.text: The premise describes what the Heroes are doing in the series. Some of the more common premises for series are described below, but these are only ideas. Some of the premises below are closely related to certain heroic motivations set forth in Chapter 2. This should not affect the motivations players select for their Heroes. A Hero’s motivation is about them; it does not need to tie-in to the overall premise of a series. Like many works of fiction, comic books are full of characters with disparate motivations who nevertheless band together for a singular purpose.

sections.heading: ADVENTURE
sections.text: The Heroes are adventurers, traveling wherever their fortunes may lead them. Their heroics come from helping those they encounter on their journeys.

sections.heading: CONSPIRACY
sections.text: This series appears to be something else at the start, but over time, the Heroes slowly become aware that something terrible is happening and nothing is as it seems. These series can evolve into anything, but they usually move in the direction of comedy, horror, or intrigue.

sections.heading: ESPIONAGE
sections.text: The Heroes are secret agents working for the government or some noble independent organization. These series often pit the Heroes against agents of an evil spy organization.

sections.heading: FREELANCERS
sections.text: The Heroes are private detectives, heroes-for-hire, or soldiers of fortune, and the series follows their adventures as they help those in need of their unique abilities.

sections.heading: FUGITIVES
sections.text: This series involves Heroes on the wrong side of the law, doing what they can to fight the power, or maybe just to survive. The Heroes are often criminals by virtue of their special gifts, because they belong to a hated or oppressed group, because they steal from the rich and give to the poor, etc.

sections.heading: GOTHIC UNDERWORLD
sections.text: The Heroes are monsters of myth and legend, beings like vampires, werewolves, ghosts, goblins, fairies, and the like, making their way among a (mostly) clueless human populace.

sections.heading: LAW ENFORCEMENT
sections.text: The Heroes are members of a law enforcement agency, and the series involves the usual elements like investigating crimes, chasing criminals, and going undercover.

sections.heading: MILITARY
sections.text: The Heroes are members of a military or paramilitary organization. Some of these series pit the Heroes against an evil paramilitary organization or an alien or extradimensional invasion. Others have the Heroes working for a rebellion against an evil empire. And others involve an actual historical war.

sections.heading: NOBLES
sections.text: The Heroes are members of a royal line or a unique lineage that grants them their abilities, and the series concerns them carrying out the obligations that are their birthright.

sections.heading: ORDINARY FOLKS
sections.text: The Heroes were ordinary people who recently developed or discovered their powers and are now trying to understand what this means for themselves and their families.

sections.heading: SUPERHEROES
sections.text: The Heroes are individuals who for various reasons have banded together—or will band together at the start of the series—to protect the innocent and combat the forces of evil.

sections.heading: MOOD
sections.text: Mood describes the general tone and feel of your series. Is it silly and lighthearted, dark and serious, or somewhere in between? Just because a series has a mood doesn’t mean that every scene of every story should share that mood. That should never be the case. You need contrast to make things stand out. Even the darkest series should have moments of happiness or levity, and even the lightest should have its serious or sad moments. As with the setting, you should discuss the game’s mood with your players ahead of time. If everyone wants lots of angst, they probably won’t be satisfied with a four-color heroic slugfest played mostly for laughs. To keep things simple, mood is broken down into five categories: bleak, dark, standard, light, and comedic. Each is described below.

sections.heading: BLEAK
sections.text: The series is extremely cynical, grim, and almost hopeless. The optional Gritty Combat Rules are pretty much required, as death and tragedy will probably be all-too common.

sections.heading: DARK
sections.text: The series is somber, or at least serious, and will probably deal with issues and involve conflicts deeper and more complex than simple good guys versus bad guys. At least some of the optional Gritty Combat Rules may be appropriate to underscore the fact that this isn’t all fun and games.

sections.heading: STANDARD
sections.text: The series is neither especially dark nor light, but individual stories may vary. Overall, it will probably be on par with most major comic book titles and all but the darkest comic book movies.

sections.heading: LIGHT
sections.text: The series is lighthearted, about on par with the average superhero cartoon. Characters never get seriously hurt, much less killed, and heavy topics or moral quandaries are generally avoided or given only the slightest nod. There may be ups and downs, but everything will turn out alright in the end.

sections.heading: COMEDIC
sections.text: The series is not at all serious and may well be played purely for laughs. Although comedic one-shots can be fun, it can be difficult to maintain this mood over a series of any real length.

sections.heading: HEROES
sections.text: No, this isn’t where you create the Heroes. You might create Heroes for a one-shot, or maybe for a game you plan to run at a convention, but not for an ongoing series. It’s always better to let players create their own Heroes so they’ll be invested in them right from the start. Instead, what you need to do as GM is help set the ground rules regarding the kinds of Heroes that will be suitable for the game.

sections.heading: POWER LEVEL
sections.text: The first thing you need to do is select a power level. Will the Heroes be street-level prowlers, paragons with godlike abilities, or somewhere in between? This depends on what the Heroes will be doing and what kind of adversaries they’ll be facing. As discussed in Chapter 2, this also determines the game’s Trait Cap and the number of Hero Points the players have to create their characters. It’s important to understand that these numbers are somewhat arbitrary. If you want to give your players 100 or 150 Hero Points instead of the usual 125 Hero Points in a Standard game with a 12d Trait Cap, feel free to do so. Hero points exist to maintain some level of balance among the Heroes, so the exact number is less important than the fact that all Heroes have the same amount.

sections.heading: TRAIT CAP
sections.text: Whatever your game’s power level or starting Hero Points may be, keep an eye on abilities that work in tandem or grant flat bonuses. Even when a Hero’s ranks fall within the game’s Trait Cap, Powers like Growth and Shrinking can push a Hero’s effective rank over the edge. As the GM, feel free to restrict any combination of Abilities, Talents, and Powers that effectively exceeds the game’s Trait Cap. On the other hand, the Trait Cap isn’t set in stone. It matters when dealing with attacks, defenses, and Traits that affect other characters. However, certain Powers aren’t particularly gamebreaking at any rank. For example, 12d Teleportation lets you travel 100 miles. If a player in a game with a 12d Trait Cap wants to be able to teleport anywhere in the world, there’s no real reason to say no, even though that requires a Teleportation rank of 18d. Sure, the Hero can travel farther in a single jump. But so what? On the other end of the spectrum, a Hero with 15d Armor, Might, or (heaven forbid) Mind Control in a game with a 12d Trait Cap will have an unbalancing impact on the game and should not be permitted.

sections.heading: SUITABILITY
sections.text: The other thing to consider is the kind of Heroes that fit your series. Heroes have to fit not only the setting but also the mood of your game. For example, an alien explorer doesn’t fit the setting of an American Old West game, and a Mystery Man styled pulp detective doesn’t fit the setting of a star-spanning game about Heroes that protect the galaxy. Similarly, a deeply troubled and emotionally scarred addict doesn’t fit the mood of a light-hearted game based on Saturday morning cartoons, and a bubbly Anime-inspired magic schoolgirl doesn’t fit the mood of a gritty game about low-powered supers operating in occupied France during the Second World War. To avoid conflicts like these, make sure your players understand the mood and setting of the game you intend to run.

sections.heading: METAPLOT
sections.text: The last thing to consider is whether your game will have a metaplot, an overarching storyline that unfolds over the course of the series. If so, you should give some thought to how much of an impact you want that metaplot to have in the game. As with everything else, there are tradeoffs. Some series are metaplot heavy, with a tight plotline that unfolds over the course of the campaign. Most stories involve the metaplot in some way, directly or indirectly advancing it towards its eventual climax and resolution. The series may include occasional interludes that aren’t related to the metaplot, but these will be rare. This kind of series allows you and your players to tell an epic story, but it can be tedious if the series goes on too long. Worse, if handled improperly, these series can make players feel like they’re being told a story rather than helping to create one. Other series are metaplot light, with a loose plotline that unfolds over the course of the campaign but doesn’t intrude itself into every story. Some stories will involve the metaplot and others won’t. This kind of series also lets you and your players tell an epic story, but it doesn’t bash you over the head with it. It gives players more freedom to do whatever they want with their Heroes because not every story is going to involve some grand overarching plotline. The downside, however, is that it takes much longer to tell a truly epic story in this kind of game. And last, some series have no metaplot at all. In series like these, the game moves from one story to the next and ends when everyone tires of it. The stories in this kind of series are selfcontained, having little connection to those that come before it or those that follow. The only common threads in these stories are the Heroes themselves and maybe some recurring NPCs. The advantage of this kind of series is that the Heroes are free to do anything they want without fear of derailing the game. The disadvantage is that series like these can feel aimless. Without the progression of a larger story, these series can start to feel like a mindless exercise in beating up one Villain after another.

sections.heading: NARRATIVE TECHNIQUES
sections.text: Writers use a variety of narrative techniques to make their stories more interesting. Although this is a game and not a story, some of these techniques translate well into roleplaying. While you shouldn’t overuse them, these techniques can make your games more entertaining and memorable.

sections.heading: CLIFFHANGERS
sections.text: There’s no better way to end an issue than with a cliffhanger. A cliffhanger is a classic trope in which one episode or issue ends with the Heroes in serious trouble or discovering some shocking revelation. Because this happens at the end of the game, the players can’t do anything about it until the next time they play. Ideally, this should create excitement and anticipation for the next game, and one issue’s cliffhanger can get the next issue off to a great start.

sections.heading: CONTRAST
sections.text: Contrast intensifies the effect of whatever you want to highlight, especially when it comes to a scene’s mood or pace. If you want to make something about a scene really stand out or feel more powerful, do the exact opposite in the previous scene. For example, if you have a scene in which the Heroes are going to receive some depressing news, make sure they’re happy and having fun right before that happens. Similarly, if the Heroes are going to be pulled into a frantic chase in one scene, make sure the scene before that is a bit more low-key. The players will feel the difference.

sections.heading: CUT SCENES
sections.text: A cut scene is a brief scene that isn’t about the Heroes. It tells the players something about the story the Heroes don’t know and can’t act on. Just like when you’re reading a comic book in which you know something the Heroes don’t, this can create tension and make the story more interesting. For example, a cut scene can let the players know that their Heroes have only a limited amount of time to accomplish some objective. Or it can show the main Villain doing something that tells the players how powerful, how evil, or even—and this one will really throw your players for a loop—how sympathetic a character the Villain really is. You might even try to get all artsy and use cut scenes to juxtapose something happening elsewhere in the game world with what the Heroes are doing. Juxtaposition can be tricky and has a very high potential cheese factor, though, so be careful with it. Whatever the case, most cut scenes should be very brief. Give the players a quick description of what happens in the cut scene and then get right back to the Heroes. No one wants to watch you put on a one-man or one-woman show, not even your mother. If you really want to engage your players in a cut scene, have them play the scene out (see Playing Other Characters below). The one downside of a cut scene is that it breaks immersion. It takes the players out of their Heroes’ heads and turns them into an audience. It shows the players things their Heroes haven’t seen or gives them information their Heroes don’t know. For these reasons, some GMs don’t use cut scenes, preferring instead to let the players experience the game world only through their Heroes. There’s no right or wrong here; it’s a matter of personal preference.

sections.heading: FORESHADOWING
sections.text: Foreshadowing is a tricky technique that’s easy to use but hard to use well. It involves dropping hints about something that will happen later in the game but making those hints too subtle for the players to figure out what’s being foreshadowed. The players aren’t supposed to notice these hints, much less figure out what they mean. The hints should just sit there, in the background, ignored by everyone until whatever has been foreshadowed occurs. When it does, the players should look back and see that those hints were staring them in the face all along. If it’s done right, foreshadowing can be tremendously powerful and make for a truly memorable game.

sections.heading: INTERLUDES
sections.text: An interlude is a scene that involves one or more of the Heroes but isn’t related to the plot of the story. Interludes provide a break in the action and afford the players an opportunity to roleplay their Heroes in their daily lives, giving them a bit more depth. Interludes can range from brief moments of comic relief to major subplots that get played out over multiple stories and forever alter a Hero’s life. Unlike the other techniques in this section, players create interludes. Players are encouraged to design interludes for their Heroes and present them to the GM. If they wish, two or more players can join forces and create an interlude that involves multiple Heroes. GMs should run these interludes by fitting them into the game whenever they can and adding their own ideas into the mix. If players don’t like how their interlude is going, they can put it on hold and discuss it with the GM at the end of the issue. The two can then either modify the interlude or cancel it at the player’s discretion (players have complete authority over their interludes). As a reward for adding to the narrative, players earn 1 Resolve whenever their interludes get played out during an issue. Each Hero is allowed only one interlude (or one joint interlude) per story, and GMs should usually run no more than one or two interludes per issue. There are many different types of interludes, but some of the more common ones are listed below.

sections.heading: CIVIC DUTY
sections.text: The Hero performs a minor civic or heroic activity that doesn’t involve thwarting some grand plot, something like foiling a purse snatching, getting a cat out of a tree, making a charity appearance, or speaking to a group of kids. We get to see the character be heroic in an everyday setting.

sections.heading: COMIC RELIEF
sections.text: Something funny or embarrassing happens to the Hero. This is a great way to add some depth to serious Heroes and grim loner types. You may be the best there is at what you do, and it may not be very pretty, but if you have to do it in a pink bunny suit, we’re still going to laugh at you.

sections.heading: FLASHBACK
sections.text: This interlude can involve just about anything, but it usually concerns a situation that happened in the past and somehow relates to the current story. When the GM runs a flashback, it’s usually to provide players with clues or details for the larger story. When a flashback is played as an interlude, however, its main purpose is to tell us something about the Heroes.

sections.heading: FRIEND IN NEED
sections.text: One of the Hero’s civilian friends needs mundane help of the real-life variety. Maybe the friend is addicted to alcohol or drugs, is facing a divorce, got kicked out of school, or was fired from their job. This kind of interlude helps us get to know the person behind the mask. This is a great interlude to happen between Heroes, especially when one is struggling with a personal sacrifice of the kind discussed earlier.

sections.heading: PERSONAL TRIUMPH
sections.text: Something wonderful occurs in the Hero’s personal life. Maybe the Hero gets married, has a child, gets accepted into the college of their dreams, wins that big promotion, or finally finishes writing that stupid roleplaying game they’ve been working on for so long. Just like Friend in Need, this interlude helps turn the Hero into something more than a two-dimensional guy or gal in a mask.

sections.heading: PERSONAL TROUBLE
sections.text: The Hero faces a tragedy like the death or severe illness of a loved one. Or maybe the Hero has to deal with a serious life issue such as marital troubles, getting fired, being kicked out of school, or deciding to write a second edition of that stupid roleplaying game. This kind of interlude shows us how the Hero deals with problems that can’t be fixed with superpowers.

sections.heading: ROMANCE
sections.text: The Hero meets someone who makes them feel all warm and fuzzy inside. The subject of the crush may or may not reciprocate. If they do, sure, they’re probably a Villain. But maybe not, and unless and until that revelation occurs, this interlude shows us the softer side of even the darkest Hero.

sections.heading: PLAYING OTHER CHARACTERS
sections.text: While it may sound strange, occasionally having the players run characters other than their Heroes can be fun. Depending on the game, the players might run these other characters for one scene, several scenes, or even an entire issue. You shouldn’t do this too often, but it can be a wonderful change of pace. As with cut scenes, not all GMs like this technique because it also breaks immersion. But if you want to try it, consider the following ways of using this technique in your games.

sections.heading: ALTERED STATES
sections.text: The players run different versions of their Heroes living in an alternate time, world, or dimension. Often, the idea behind an altered states story is that the players are actually running their Heroes, who will end up having to fix whatever went wrong with the world so that it returns to normal.

sections.heading: FLASHBACK
sections.text: The Heroes relive something that happened in the past. This sometimes occurs in cut scenes spread over the course of a story occurring in the present. The connection between the flashback and the present can be obvious from the start, or it might be revealed as the story progresses.

sections.heading: OTHER LIVES
sections.text: Often used for an entire story, the players run other characters in the past or the future and eventually learn that those characters are their Heroes in their past or future lives. Yes, it’s corny, but this is a game about comic book superheroes, and this technique can make for some cheesy fun.

sections.heading: VICTIMS
sections.text: The players begin a new story running characters other than their Heroes. These characters are eventually kidnapped, killed, or whatever. Once this happens, the players switch to their regular Heroes, who get tasked with finding out what happened to the original characters.

sections.heading: VILLAINS
sections.text: Some of the most interesting stories in comic books focus on the Villains rather than the Heroes. The same applies to roleplaying, especially when you ask players to run Villains they really hate, people who’ve made their lives miserable (the longer the better). To be effective, this technique requires mature players who are willing to take this seriously and play these characters well.

sections.heading: SPOTLIGHTING
sections.text: Whenever you have a comic about a group of superheroes, not every story can be about every character. Some stories are about the group. Others spotlight a particular character, focusing primarily on them over the course of that story. Your games can work the same way. When using this technique, some stories will involve all the Heroes equally, while others will revolve around specific Heroes. These spotlighting stories might involve the Hero’s nemesis, their family or friends, something from their past, or their long-term goals. This is much easier to do when your players give you information to work with, which is why Heroes have connections, details, and an origin. You should take turns spotlighting Heroes, focusing on one per story. Over time, every Hero will get to be in the spotlight, and every Hero’s goals and backstories will become an integral part of your series. As mentioned above, don’t feel obligated to spotlight a Hero in every story. You can if you wish, but you can also mix stories that spotlight one Hero with those that involve all the Heroes equally. In fact, this latter approach makes the spotlighting stories that much more compelling. Just be sure to give every Hero equal treatment when using this technique.

sections.heading: GAMEMASTER TIPS
sections.text: A great GM can make any story interesting and fun. Unfortunately, the art of being a great GM is just that: an art. It’s something you learn over time and never perfect. While you can learn a lot from reading about it or watching other people run games, the best way to hone your skills as a GM is to run a lot of games, make a lot of mistakes, and get a lot of feedback. With that in mind, the following tips and suggestions should be thought of as guidelines to help you move through the cycle of falling down and getting back up again on your road to being a great GM.

sections.heading: COMIC BOOK HEROES
sections.text: Always remember that the Heroes are the main characters of the series. No other characters should be anywhere near as important to the game. The Heroes must be the ones to save the world, even if they aren’t the ones who run it. They must be the ones to fire the shot that destroys the giant space station, even if they aren’t the ones who planned the attack. And they must be the ones to fend off the evil cosmic entity, even if they aren’t nearly as powerful as the good cosmic entity who—for whatever reason—can only advise them and then sit back on their cosmic couch with some low-fat cosmic popcorn to watch what happens. The Heroes don’t have to be the most powerful or influential people in the game world. They usually aren’t. What they are, however, is the focus of the series. If the players ever tell you they feel overshadowed by one of your NPCs, listen to them. And remove that NPC from the game.

sections.heading: FAIRNESS
sections.text: As GM, you are the referee of the game. You oversee the application of the rules and determine when they need to be bent, broken, or ignored. This means you must be fair and consistent. While you might occasionally bend the rules, this should be to further the story, make the game more exciting, or give a new player a break (which we encourage). However, you must be a neutral arbiter, favoring neither the Heroes nor their adversaries. If you always favor the Heroes, the players won’t feel challenged and will eventually get bored. If you always favor the Villains, the players won’t feel empowered and will eventually get disheartened. Neither result is good.

sections.heading: IMPROVISING
sections.text: At some point, your players will go completely off the rails. They’ll breeze through what should have been a whole night’s worth of story in under an hour, or they’ll spend an entire night following a red herring. They’ll be stumped by a simple puzzle, or they’ll solve a convoluted mystery the moment they find the first clue. They’ll struggle against a sad little group of Minions, then plow through your toughest Villains without working up a sweat. This is when roleplaying becomes something more than acting or war gaming; this is when it really becomes an exercise in cooperative, improvisational storytelling. One of the most entertaining things about roleplaying is that you never know what to expect, whether as a player or a GM. Any good story that doesn’t involve railroading the Heroes from one scene to the next will give your players countless opportunities to catch you off guard. No matter how well prepared you think you are, your players will do things you didn’t expect. When that occurs, you’re going to have to wing it and improvise what happens next. The more you GM, the more you’ll come to relish these moments as the most exciting part of running a game. But whether you fear or love them, these moments will happen, so be prepared, be flexible, and be ready to improvise.

sections.heading: KEEP IT MOVING
sections.text: This is an action-adventure roleplaying game about superpowered Heroes and Villains. It’s neither a tactical war game nor a detailed simulation of anything in the real world. The goal is to have fun, not to win the game or determine how things might play out in real life, so speed is more important than precision. Know the rules and understand how they work. Know the story you’re going to run. And be ready to make judgment calls on the fly. That’s your job as GM. Your goal is to facilitate the game, not delay it, so spend as little time as possible checking your notes or flipping through the rules at the table. Never let the game come to a grinding halt while you look something up. If you can find what you need quickly, great. But if not, then just make a judgment call and move on. Don’t let yourself be rushed, but keep the game moving. If you discover that you’ve made a mistake, that’s fine too. Acknowledge it, remember it for the future, and you’re good.

sections.heading: METAGAMING
sections.text: Metagaming means using information you know but your character doesn’t when playing the game. The term often applies to players, but GMs can also be accused of metagaming when running NPCs. Although this opinion isn’t universal, metagaming is typically considered bad form. It’s viewed as cheating because you’re basing a character’s actions or decisions on information they have no way of knowing. To some extent, this destroys the verisimilitude of the game. When a character’s actions are determined by what the GM or the player knows rather than by what the character knows, it shatters the illusion of playing an imaginary character in an imaginary world. For example, if one of your players accidentally sees your notes and learns where to find a Villain’s secret lair, that player’s Hero can’t act on that information. Similarly, even though you as the GM know all there is to know about the Heroes, it would be unfair for your NPCs to act on that information. In both cases, metagaming is basically cheating, taking advantage of things a character shouldn’t know. Because this is a game, however, there are times when metagaming is not only acceptable, but helpful. For example, when the Heroes meet for the first time, everyone should understand they’re going to need to come together. Sure, they may not all like or trust each other right from the get-go. But the Heroes are going to have to band together eventually, and everyone must be willing to nudge their Heroes in that direction. Other examples of good metagaming by players include taking obvious plot hooks and trying to avoid splitting the team (which is a good way to get things done in real life, but a bad idea in a roleplaying game for several reasons, the greatest of which is that a GM can only pay attention to one group at a time, leaving everyone else sitting around doing nothing in the meanwhile). In cases like this, metagaming isn’t cheating and doesn’t have a negative impact on the game. On the contrary, it serves to help the game along and is therefore encouraged.

sections.heading: PROPS
sections.text: Although they’re entirely optional, physical props can add a wonderful touch to almost any game. Because most of what happens in the game takes place in the imagination, there’s something very powerful about what amounts to pulling a tangible object out of the game world and handing it to the players. Story elements such as written orders, newspaper clippings, photographs, letters, scraps of paper, half-burned journal entries, and encoded messages are all more interesting when players can actually hold them in their hands, read them for themselves, or hear them. And players always appreciate the effort put into buying or making even the cheesiest prop. If you have the time and inclination, you should always consider how you might bring a prop or two into your games.

sections.heading: RAILROADING
sections.text: Railroading is when a GM sets the game up in such a way that the players must follow a specific course of action. This usually involves actions that move the plot in a specific direction, but it can also take the form of obstacles or puzzles that can only be overcome in one specific way (determined by the GM ahead of time). As you probably suspect, railroading is generally frowned upon because it robs players of the only thing they are allowed to do in the game: control their Heroes. It turns what should be a game into an interactive story and the GM into a storyteller. This is boring and frustrating for the players, who are there to play, not to see the GM perform. If you ever feel compelled to railroad your players, stop the game. Literally stop the game and take a break. It means your players caught you off guard and are doing something you didn’t expect. Take a moment to regroup and consider what will happen after they do what they want rather than what you expected. Instead of getting upset that they’re ruining your story, remind yourself that once you started playing the game, the story became theirs too, and everyone now has an equal say in how it turns out. And remind yourself that this, in fact, is what keeps the game exciting for you as GM. There’s one exception to the “no railroading” rule, at least when it comes to this genre. GMs should feel free to put the Heroes in just about any situation they wish at the beginning of a new story. Stories should start off with a bang, immediately drawing the players into the action. Sometimes, this means GMs determine what happened (and what the Heroes were doing) before the first scene opens. Superhero comics grew out of the pulps, a genre of contrived plots and unlikely coincidences, and the apple didn’t fall far from the tree. Accordingly, players need to be okay with a little introductory railroading. While a GM should never have the Heroes do anything absurdly stupid or wildly out of character, players should give their GMs some leeway when it comes to getting a new story rolling.

sections.heading: ROLLING THE DICE
sections.text: It may sound strange but knowing when you shouldn’t roll dice is at least as important as knowing when you should. Obviously, you roll dice whenever you need to determine the result of an action whose outcome is uncertain. Uncertainty, however, isn’t the only thing to consider when determining whether to roll dice. The other things to keep in mind are whether the action is relevant to the game, and whether the game will keep moving forward regardless of the outcome. Don’t make players roll to determine the results of trivial or inconsequential actions. Similarly, don’t make them roll to obtain information that fleshes out a story and makes everything more interesting but has no bearing on the game. Lousy games are choked with rolls to determine whether Heroes can accomplish every little task, or to see if they know some tidbit of backstory. Don’t run a lousy game. Any time you’re about to ask a player to make a roll, ask yourself if there’s any reason not to just let the player succeed. If there isn’t, if the roll’s success or failure won’t impact the drama or the excitement of the game in any real way, then let the Hero accomplish the trivial task or give them the information and move on. On the flipside, don’t make players roll for any action that must go a certain way to keep the story moving. If the Heroes need to find a clue to reach the next part of the story, let them find it (thank you, Robin Laws). If you paint yourself into a corner from which you can’t escape unless a Hero either makes or fails a roll, don’t bother asking for a roll to create the illusion of choice. Instead, just take control of the story, narrate what happens in that moment, and give the Hero 1 point of Resolve. Mind you, this kind of thing shouldn’t happen. You should try to avoid these situations by creating flexible stories focused on problems rather than solutions (leave the solutions to the Heroes). But nobody’s perfect. If it happens to you, don’t try to fake your way around it. Just fess up, pay up, and move on.

sections.heading: SAYING YES
sections.text: When a player asks if they can do something, or at least try something, your impulse should be to say yes. This is especially true if what they want to attempt is cool. If your impulse is to say no, ask yourself why. Are you saying no because what the player is suggesting is completely out of the question, or because you’ve been caught off guard? Often, it’s the latter: a player hits you with an idea you aren’t prepared to handle, so you just say no. While that impulse is understandable, don’t give in to it. Instead, take a few minutes to collect your thoughts and see if you can find a way to handle whatever the player just tossed in your lap. Odds are you can. Then let the player try. Remember that the Heroes in this game are superheroes. They’re supposed to be able to do ridiculous things, or at least try them. Don’t forget that just because you get caught off guard.

sections.heading: PLAYER TIPS
sections.text: Everything in this chapter has been about the GM, which makes sense since so much of the game rests on their shoulders. But the GM is just one person, and one person can’t be responsible for everyone’s fun. The GM is usually going to be outnumbered by the players, so this last section includes a few tips for players, things every GM should reasonably expect.

sections.heading: DON’T ARGUE
sections.text: As the referee, your GM is constantly deciding how to apply the rules and making judgement calls about how things work and what is and isn’t possible in the game. If you think your GM has made a mistake in their application of the rules or you disagree with one of their calls, tell them and explain why. But once you’ve shared your opinion and your GM makes a final decision, it’s time to move on. If you disagree, discuss this during the next break or after the game ends for the night. Don’t bring the game to a grinding halt by debating any point at the table. Even if you’re right, it isn’t worth the delay.

sections.heading: DON’T CHEAT
sections.text: It’s amazing that some people cheat while roleplaying, especially when you consider that there’s nothing at stake and no way to win the game. It’s natural not to want to see your Hero stumble, be made the fool, or get defeated. But don’t cheat. First, it’s stupid. Honestly, it just is. Apart from that, the longer you play games like this, the more you come to realize that failure is often more interesting than success. Some of your best gaming stories are going to come from when your Hero really blows it. Roll the dice and let them fall where they may. Trust us: you’ll have a lot more fun.

sections.heading: FOCUS
sections.text: Pay attention to the game, even when you aren’t directly involved in the action. Nothing makes a GM feel less appreciated than seeing players flip through the rules, watch TV, or play around on their laptops or phones. It’s utterly disheartening. Being a GM is like being a combination performer, storyteller, and tour guide, and nothing makes a GM feel worse than when their players look bored. Plus, players who tune out often miss important clues and information. If you aren’t interested in the game, don’t play. If you need a break, take one. But if you’re there to play, then give the game your attention.

sections.heading: GO WITH IT
sections.text: Creating a memorable roleplaying experience takes cooperation between the GM and the players, but the person who makes the first move is usually the GM, so help yours out when you can. When the GM tosses a plot hook your way, take the bait and get the story going. If you know your GM wants you to do something or go somewhere, try to go with the narrative rather than resist it. Of course, you shouldn’t do anything out of character just to appease the GM. But when you see a clear plot hook sitting in front of you, instead of asking yourself whether you would take the bait, maybe assume that you will, and instead ask yourself why. Whenever possible, remember you’re playing a game in which everyone has at least some responsibility to go with the flow of the collective narrative.

sections.heading: HELP OUT
sections.text: GMs have a hard job. They come up with stories for the Heroes to experience, create and run all characters who aren’t Heroes, and oversee the application of the rules. That’s a lot to handle, so try to help your GM whenever you can. If they’re struggling to keep everyone’s attention focused on the game, help them get the other players on track. If your GM is flipping through the rules, ask if you can help. Maybe you know where to find whatever it is they need. If your GM seems unsure about how to handle a situation, throw out some suggestions. In short, try to make life easier for the poor soul.

sections.heading: IMAGINE
sections.text: Roleplaying is an exercise in make-believe. If you use your imagination, it can take you anywhere you want to go and let you do anything you want to do. If you don’t, it will bore you to tears. Imagination is crucial when roleplaying. Unlike video games, which display imaginary worlds, roleplaying games suggest them. Just like when you’re reading a book, many of the details are up to you. Always use your imagination and try to picture what’s happening in the game world while roleplaying. Otherwise, the experience becomes nothing more than a few hours spent rolling dice and doing basic math.

sections.heading: PARTICIPATE
sections.text: Your GM can’t be expected to do everything. It’s up to you to participate. Don’t sit there silently waiting for someone to tell you what to do. Speak up and interact with the GM and the other players. Play your Hero, suggest solutions to whatever problems your GM throws at you, and get into the game. If you’re new to the game (or the hobby, for that matter), don’t worry about the rules; your GM and fellow players are there to help you. Be an active participant, not a passive observer. However, be careful not to go too far and hog the spotlight or the GM’s attention. Let other players, especially new ones, play their Heroes, come up with ideas, and participate in the game as well.

sections.heading: ROLEPLAY
sections.text: It’s called a roleplaying game for a reason. The whole point of the game is to pretend to be someone else, so go for it. Get into your Hero’s head and try to act, think, and even talk like that imaginary person. The beauty of roleplaying is that it lets you step into someone else’s shoes, someone who may be very different from you. Take the opportunity and play that other person to the hilt, even if that leads you to do or say things you never would. That’s what this is all about.

sections.heading: SAVOR CHALLENGES
sections.text: Your GM is supposed to challenge you. When things get tough, don’t get so frustrated that you just toss your hands in the air and concede defeat. Don’t get mad at your GM, even if things look bleak or you find yourself out of ideas. Your GM isn’t trying to make your life miserable (well, probably not). They’re just trying to create an exciting story, which means it can’t be a cakewalk. Sometimes things are going to look bad for the Heroes. Those moments are priceless. When that happens, savor the tension. Don’t lose sight of the fact that it’s just a game, don’t take things personally, and don’t forget that the actual goal of the game is to have a good time with your friends.
